Epidemiology & Risk Factors.title: Gynecologic Cancer Epidemiology & Risk Factors
Epidemiology & Risk Factors.html:
A woman with a GYN cancer walks into your clinic. The first question is which organ, because "GYN" is really several diseases that share the pelvis but have different causes, patients, and treatments. For each one, ask four things: what causes it, who gets it, how it presents, and why that matters for treatment.

HPV below (cervix, vagina, many vulvar cancers). Estrogen above, for endometrioid endometrial cancer. Genes for ovary (BRCA).

That line is a starting framework, not the whole story. HPV is central to many lower genital tract cancers, but endometrial cancer is biologically heterogeneous: obesity and unopposed estrogen explain most endometrioid tumors, while serous and p53-abnormal tumors are not estrogen-driven and behave far more aggressively.

The Big Picture

SiteWhat causes itWho gets itHow it presentsWhy that matters for treatment
CervixHPVYounger women, often under-screenedPostcoital or irregular bleedingEarly disease: surgery or RT. Locally advanced: chemoradiation + brachytherapy
EndometriumUnopposed estrogen (endometrioid); p53 and other molecular pathways; LynchPostmenopausal, often with obesity or diabetesPostmenopausal bleeding, so usually found earlySurgery first; RT or systemic therapy based on recurrence risk
VulvaHPV or lichen sclerosusOlder womenItching, a lump, or an ulcerSurgery with groin staging; RT for nodes or margins, or chemoRT when surgery would be mutilating
VaginaHPV; DES (clear cell)Older womenBleeding or dischargeRT is the main treatment (EBRT + brachytherapy)
OvaryBRCA1/2, LynchPostmenopausalVague bloating, often advanced at diagnosisSurgery and chemotherapy; RT mostly palliative

Cervical Cancer

1
HPV

Found in nearly all cervical cancers, with HPV 16 and 18 causing most of them. Sexually transmitted.

2
Persistence

Smoking and immunosuppression (HIV, transplant) keep the virus from clearing. More exposure (more partners, early first intercourse) raises risk.

3
Missed Screening

Lack of screening is the biggest modifiable risk. Many patients with locally advanced disease simply never had access to screening.

4
DES

In utero diethylstilbestrol exposure: clear cell carcinoma of the cervix and vagina, the classic non-HPV exception.

  • Prevention: the HPV vaccine prevents new infections. Screening (cytology and/or HPV testing) finds precancer before it becomes cancer. Vaccinated women still need screening.
  • Presentation: postcoital or irregular bleeding and discharge; later pelvic or back pain, leg swelling, or kidney failure from a blocked ureter.
1
HPV-associated
→
2
Screening and vaccine prevent it
→
3
Presents with abnormal or postcoital bleeding
→
4
Locally advanced disease: definitive chemoRT + brachytherapy
Reference: vaccine and screening schedules▾
  • 9-valent HPV vaccine: routine at 11–12, catch-up through 26; 27–45 by shared decision-making.
  • USPSTF screening: 21–29, cytology every 3 years. 30–65, cytology every 3 years, hrHPV every 5 years, or co-testing every 5 years. Over 65 with adequate negative screening: stop.
Clinical Pearl

The HPV vaccine prevents new infections but doesn't clear existing ones. That's why vaccinated women still get screened.

Endometrial Cancer

For endometrioid cancer, the central risk factor is unopposed estrogen: estrogen stimulating the endometrium without progesterone to balance it. It explains most of the classic risk factors:

1
Physiologic

Obesity (fat converts androgens to estrogen; the strongest modifiable factor), nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause.

2
Medical

PCOS (anovulation), diabetes, estrogen-secreting tumors (granulosa cell).

3
Medications

Unopposed estrogen HRT and tamoxifen (an estrogen agonist in the uterus).

4
Genetics

Lynch syndrome (mismatch repair deficiency) greatly raises lifetime risk. Every endometrial cancer is tested for MMR/MSI.

  • Protective: combined oral contraceptives, progestin IUD, pregnancy.
  • Presentation: postmenopausal bleeding, so most cancers are found while still confined to the uterus. Work it up with a transvaginal ultrasound (a thickened stripe, over about 4 mm, needs tissue) and an endometrial biopsy.
  • Precursor: atypical hyperplasia (EIN) often has a coexisting cancer, so it's usually treated with hysterectomy.
Classic "Type I"
Endometrioid, low grade

Estrogen-driven, often obese patients, arises from hyperplasia, good prognosis.

Classic "Type II"
Serous, clear cell, high grade

Not estrogen-driven, older and often thinner patients, p53-mutated, spreads early (peritoneum), poor prognosis.

The Molecular Groups: Why They Matter

The old Type I/II split is being replaced by four molecular groups. Don't just memorize best to worst; the point is that molecular classification increasingly modifies recurrence-risk assessment and the choice of adjuvant treatment, and modern FIGO staging uses it in selected early stages.

GroupBehaviorHow it can change the plan
POLE-mutatedVery low recurrence risk, even if high gradeA candidate for de-escalation of adjuvant therapy
MMR-deficientIntermediateLynch screening; responds well to immunotherapy in advanced disease
p53-abnormalAggressive, even when confined to the uterusA reason to escalate (chemotherapy ± RT)
No specific molecular profile (NSMP)IntermediateClassic pathology (grade, depth, LVSI) drives the decision

Vulvar and Vaginal Cancer

HPV-associated
Younger women

HSIL/usual-type VIN, smoking, immunosuppression, often other HPV cancers (cervix, anus). Better prognosis.

HPV-independent
Older women

Arises in lichen sclerosus through differentiated VIN. p53-mutated, worse prognosis.

  • Vulvar cancer presents with itching, a lump, or an ulcer, often after months of treatment for "irritation." Biopsy any persistent vulvar lesion.
  • Most arise on the labia majora; midline tumors (clitoris, perineum) drain to both groins.
  • Vaginal cancer is rare. A vaginal tumor that also involves the cervix is staged as cervical, and one that touches the vulva as vulvar. Many tumors in the vagina are actually metastases or recurrences, so a true vaginal primary is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Self-check: a 38-year-old with endometrial cancer and a strong family history of colon cancer. What test, and why does it matter for treatment?▾

Test the tumor for mismatch repair (MMR) / MSI and refer for germline testing for Lynch syndrome. It affects her family's screening, her own colon cancer risk, and treatment: MMR-deficient tumors respond well to immunotherapy.

Self-check: a thin 74-year-old with no estrogen exposure has endometrial cancer. Does "estrogen above" fit her?▾

Not well. Think serous or p53-abnormal disease, which is not estrogen-driven, spreads early, and often needs more aggressive adjuvant therapy even when it looks confined to the uterus.

High-Yield Summary
  • Cervical cancer is caused by HPV, presents with abnormal or postcoital bleeding, and when locally advanced is usually treated with definitive chemoradiation plus brachytherapy.
  • Endometrioid endometrial cancer is driven by obesity and unopposed estrogen, but serous and p53-abnormal tumors are not estrogen-driven and behave more aggressively.
  • Endometrial cancer usually presents early with postmenopausal bleeding, so surgery is the foundation and radiation or systemic therapy is added based on recurrence risk.
  • The endometrial molecular groups (POLE-mutated, MMR-deficient, p53-abnormal, and no specific profile) increasingly change the recurrence-risk assessment and the choice of adjuvant therapy.
  • Vulvar cancer comes from HPV in younger women or lichen sclerosus in older women, and the lichen sclerosus type has a worse prognosis.

Anatomy & Lymphatics.title: Female Pelvic Anatomy & Lymph Node Drainage
Anatomy & Lymphatics.html:
GYN anatomy comes down to three questions: which organ (and which part of it), what is next to it (the bladder, rectum, bowel, and the tissue beside the cervix), and where its lymph drains. Learn the organs first, then the nodes. Every later section (imaging, staging, and treatment) builds on this page.

The Organs: Uterus, Cervix, Vagina, and Vulva

The Uterus and Cervix

Picture the uterus as an upside-down pear sitting between the bladder and the rectum, usually tipped forward (anteverted) over the bladder.

  • From top to bottom: the fundus, the body (corpus), and the cervix, the narrow neck that pokes down into the vagina.
  • The wall has three layers: the endometrium (the lining), the myometrium (thick muscle), and the serosa (a thin peritoneal coat). Endometrial cancer starts in the lining and grows outward through the muscle, so these layers are the yardstick you will hear about all rotation.
  • The cervical canal runs from the internal os (where it meets the uterine body) to the external os (its opening into the vagina).
  • The canal is lined by glandular (columnar) cells and the outer cervix by squamous cells. Where they meet, the transformation zone, is where HPV does its damage and where nearly every cervical cancer starts. That is why most cervical cancers are squamous and a minority are adenocarcinomas.

The Ligaments and Parametria

The cervix is anchored in place by ligaments. They matter because tumor and lymph travel along them.

Cardinal Ligament

Runs from the cervix sideways to the pelvic side wall. The fatty tissue around it is the parametrium, which carries the uterine artery, the ureter, and lymphatics.

Uterosacral Ligament

Runs from the cervix back around the rectum to the sacrum. A lymphatic path to the presacral nodes.

Broad Ligament

A sheet of peritoneum draped over the uterus and tubes. Its infundibulopelvic part carries the ovarian vessels up toward the para-aortic region.

Round Ligament

Runs from the top corner of the uterus through the inguinal canal to the labia. A rare route to the groin nodes.

  • Cervical cancer grows sideways into the parametria, toward the side wall. That is why the rectovaginal exam and the MRI both focus on the tissue beside the cervix.
  • The ureter passes under the uterine artery about 2 cm lateral to the cervix ("water under the bridge"). Tumor growing sideways can squeeze it and back up the kidney, and this same spot is close to brachytherapy point A.

The Neighbors: Organs at Risk

Bladder

In front of the cervix and upper vagina, separated by a thin septum. Gets dose from both pelvic RT and brachytherapy.

Rectum

Behind, across the pouch of Douglas (the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity). The organ that most often limits brachytherapy dose.

Sigmoid & Small Bowel

Above the uterus; loops can drape over the brachytherapy tandem. Bowel dose limits pelvic IMRT.

Bone Marrow, Kidneys, Femoral Heads

Pelvic marrow matters with chemo, kidneys with para-aortic fields, femoral heads with groin fields.

The Vagina

A muscular tube about 7 to 9 cm long running up and back from the introitus to the cervix. At the top it forms the fornices, the recesses around the cervix where brachytherapy ovoids or a ring sit. The easiest way to remember it is in thirds, because each third has different neighbors and drains to a different place.

Part Neighbors Lymph drains to
Upper third Cervix (fornices), bladder base in front, pouch of Douglas behind Pelvic nodes, like the cervix
Middle third Bladder and urethra in front, rectum behind Pelvic nodes
Lower third Urethra in front, anal canal and perineal body behind Groin (inguinofemoral) nodes, like the vulva
  • The posterior wall sits on the rectum (the rectovaginal septum) and also drains to presacral nodes.
  • After a hysterectomy, the top of the vagina is sewn closed as the vaginal cuff. It is the most common place for endometrial cancer to recur, which is why it is the target of vaginal brachytherapy.

The Vulva

  • The external genitalia: the mons pubis, labia majora (outer, hair-bearing skin) and labia minora, the clitoris, the urethral meatus, the vaginal introitus, the Bartholin glands, and the perineal body between the vagina and anus.
  • Most vulvar cancers are squamous cancers of the labia majora. Think of the vulva as skin: it drains like skin, to the groins.
  • The midline matters. Lymph from midline structures (clitoris, perineal body) crosses to both groins. A lesion well off to one side (2 cm or more from the midline) drains mainly to one groin.
  • The urethra, vagina, and anus all sit within a few centimeters, so even modest tumors can reach them.
Self-check: a cervical cancer grows sideways and the patient's kidney on that side is now swollen on CT. What anatomy explains this?▾

The ureter runs through the parametrium, under the uterine artery about 2 cm lateral to the cervix. Tumor spreading sideways squeezes it, urine backs up, and the kidney swells (hydronephrosis).

Self-check: a vaginal tumor sits in the lower third. Which nodes are at risk?▾

The inguinofemoral (groin) nodes. The lower third drains like the vulva, so the groins are included in the RT field.

The Lymph Nodes: Drainage by Organ

Drainage by Site: Click Through Each Organ

Each Organ Drains Differently

Organ Drainage path Regional nodes Counts as distant
Cervix Parametrial → obturator, internal & external iliac → common iliac → para-aortic; presacral via the uterosacral ligaments Pelvic and para-aortic Supraclavicular, mediastinal, inguinal (unless the lower vagina is involved)
Endometrium Pelvic nodes like the cervix, plus straight to the para-aortics from the fundus (ovarian vessels); rarely inguinal via the round ligament Pelvic and para-aortic Inguinal, intra-abdominal
Ovary Mostly para-aortic (ovarian vessels); also pelvic Retroperitoneal Beyond the abdomen
Vagina Upper → pelvic; lower → inguinofemoral; posterior wall → presacral Pelvic or inguinal Beyond these
Vulva Superficial inguinal → deep femoral (Cloquet's) → external iliac Inguinofemoral only Pelvic nodes
Cervix and uterus drain mainly along pelvic and para-aortic pathways. Vulva and lower vagina drain to the groins first. For the vulva, a pelvic node is distant.

The exact nodal risk depends on where the tumor sits and how far it has spread: a fundal endometrial cancer can reach the para-aortics directly, and a cervical cancer that extends to the lower vagina adds the groins.

Turning Drainage into Fields

On a sub-I, the question is where does this cancer drain, not whether you could contour the volume tomorrow. Each field simply follows the drainage above.

FieldCoversUsed for
Pelvic fieldThe primary (or vaginal cuff) plus the pelvic nodesCervix, endometrium
Extended fieldPelvis plus the para-aortic nodesPara-aortic nodes, or high-risk common iliac disease
Pelvis + groinsPelvic nodes plus the inguinofemoral nodesCervical or vaginal cancer reaching the lower vagina
Vulva + groins ± pelvisThe vulva and inguinofemoral nodes, adding the pelvic nodes when the groins are positiveVulvar cancer
  • Vulvar sentinel node biopsy is used for small, unifocal tumors with clinically negative groins (GROINSS-V). Lateral tumors: same-side groin; midline tumors: both.
  • Groin node depth varies a lot with body size, so groin fields are planned on CT, not by a fixed depth.
Planning details: elective nodal volumes▾
  • Pelvic nodal CTV: common iliac (from about L4–L5), external and internal iliac, obturator, and presacral nodes (to about S3).
  • Extended field: adds the para-aortic nodes up to about the renal vessels (T12–L1), or above the highest involved node.
  • Vulvar sentinel node eligibility (GROINSS-V): unifocal tumor under 4 cm with clinically negative groins.

Exact boundaries come from consensus contouring atlases and vary by protocol.

High-Yield Summary
  • The uterus has a fundus, body, and cervix, and endometrial cancer starts in the lining and grows outward through the muscle wall.
  • Cervical cancer starts at the transformation zone, where the glandular cells of the canal meet the squamous cells of the outer cervix.
  • The cardinal ligaments and parametria run from the cervix to the pelvic side wall and carry the uterine artery, the ureter, and lymphatics, so tumor spreading sideways can block the ureter.
  • The upper two-thirds of the vagina drain to the pelvic nodes, while the lower third drains to the groins like the vulva.
  • Cervical and endometrial cancers drain mainly along pelvic and para-aortic pathways, while vulvar cancer spreads to the groins first and pelvic nodes count as distant.

Imaging.title: Gynecologic Imaging: MRI, PET/CT, CT & Brachytherapy
Imaging.html:
GYN imaging answers three questions, in order. Build every scan you see around them:

1
MRI: where is the tumor locally?
→
2
PET/CT: where has it spread?
→
3
CT simulation: how do I treat it safely?

For an intact cervix there is a fourth step: MRI or CT with the brachytherapy applicator in place, which is where the curative dose is shaped. This section comes before Workup & Staging because FIGO lets imaging assign the cervical stage.

QuestionTestWhat the answer changes
How big is it, and what does it touch?Pelvic MRISurgery vs chemoradiation (cervix); depth and cervical involvement (endometrium); the local target
Are there nodes or distant disease?FDG PET/CT (or CT)Nodal boosts, an extended field, or a different treatment intent
Where are the target and the organs at risk?CT simulationThe EBRT plan
Where is the residual tumor relative to the bladder, rectum, and sigmoid?MRI/CT with the applicator in placeThe brachytherapy plan, fraction by fraction

Cervical Cancer MRI: Where Is the Tumor Locally?

  • T2 is the key sequence. Tumor is intermediate (gray); the normal cervical stroma is a dark ring around it.
  • Intact dark cervical stroma = the tumor is still contained. Tumor crossing that ring into the fat beside the cervix = parametrial invasion.
  • Then walk outward: vaginal extension (upper vs lower vagina), the ureters (hydronephrosis), and the fat planes with the bladder and rectum (mucosal invasion must be confirmed with cystoscopy or proctoscopy and biopsy).
  • DWI (bright tumor, dark ADC) helps define the edges and find small nodes.
Dark ring intact = parametria clear. Ring broken = parametrial invasion, which usually means chemoradiation rather than surgery.

Endometrial Cancer MRI

  • Endometrial cancer is staged surgically, but MRI helps plan surgery and is the main staging tool for medically inoperable patients, who get definitive RT.
  • Ask two things: how deep into the myometrium (less than half vs half or more) and is the cervical stroma involved. An intact junctional zone suggests superficial disease.
  • Then look beyond the uterus: serosa, adnexa, and nodes.

Lymph Nodes on CT and PET/CT

  • Nodes are named for the vessel they sit next to, so find the vessel first, then look for a round soft-tissue nodule beside it.
  • A short axis over about 1 cm, a rounded shape, or central necrosis on CT raises concern; FDG avidity on PET/CT is more reliable than size alone.

PET/CT: Where Has It Spread?

PET/CT is the standard staging scan for locally advanced cervical cancer. Its real job is that PET changes the radiation map:

PET findingWhat happens to the plan
Pelvis PET-negativeStandard elective pelvic field
PET-positive pelvic nodePelvic field plus a boost to the node; para-aortics often added for common iliac or multiple nodes
PET-positive para-aortic nodeExtended field covering the para-aortic chain, with a boost
Distant disease (e.g., supraclavicular, lung, bone)The treatment intent may change: systemic therapy first, with RT for palliation or for selected limited disease
  • A post-treatment PET a few months after chemoRT shows whether the response is complete, which is a strong sign of a good outcome.
  • Pitfalls: physiologic bladder and ureter activity, bowel uptake, and inflammation (recent biopsy or infection).
  • Endometrial: CT (or PET/CT) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis for high-grade or suspected advanced disease; look for ascites and omental caking with serous histology.
Self-check: a 4 cm cervical cancer with a normal-sized but PET-avid common iliac node. What stage, and what field?▾

IIIC1r (common iliac is a pelvic node). Because the para-aortics are the next stop, many radiation oncologists would use an extended field, with a boost to the involved node.

CT Simulation: How Do I Treat It Safely?

  • The pelvic organs move. The uterus and cervix (or the vaginal cuff after hysterectomy) shift with bladder and rectal filling, so the team simulates and treats with a consistent, reproducible bladder and builds the target to cover that motion.
  • IMRT is standard for pelvic RT because it lowers dose to the bowel and bone marrow.
  • On the planning CT, find the target (primary or cuff plus nodes) and the organs that limit it: bladder, rectum, small bowel, bone marrow, femoral heads, and the kidneys if the field is extended.
  • Vulva: frog-leg position, and the groin nodes are contoured on CT around the femoral vessels.
Planning details: simulation setup▾
  • Intact cervix: many centers scan with a full and an empty bladder and build an ITV covering both uterine positions; the post-hysterectomy cuff is handled the same way.
  • RTOG 1203 (TIME-C): IMRT caused less GI and urinary toxicity than 3D after hysterectomy.
  • Vulva: bolus on the vulva when the skin is at risk.

Brachytherapy Imaging

This is the signature GYN radiation oncology image. The concept comes first:

1
Place the applicator (tandem + ring or ovoids, ± needles)
→
2
MRI (preferred) or CT with it in place
→
3
Contour the HR-CTV + bladder, rectum, sigmoid
→
4
Optimize tumor coverage while respecting the OARs
  • The HR-CTV is the whole cervix plus any residual tumor at the time of brachytherapy.
  • Because the tumor usually shrinks during EBRT, the brachytherapy target is smaller than at diagnosis, which is one reason imaging is repeated with each insertion.
Clinical Pearl

On the sagittal brachy MRI, check where the sigmoid sits. It can loop right over the tip of the tandem and is easy to overdose if you only look at the bladder and rectum.

Brachytherapy planning numbers: reference▾
StructureCommon goal (EQD2, EBRT + brachy combined)
HR-CTVD90 ≥85 Gy
BladderD2cc under about 80–90 Gy
RectumD2cc under about 65–75 Gy
SigmoidD2cc under about 70–75 Gy

These come from EMBRACE and vary by protocol. Point A (2 cm up and 2 cm lateral along the tandem) is the historical prescription point and is still reported for comparison.

High-Yield Summary
  • MRI answers where the tumor is locally, PET/CT answers where it has spread, and CT simulation answers how to treat it safely.
  • On T2 MRI, an intact dark cervical stromal ring means the tumor is still contained, and tumor crossing that ring means parametrial invasion.
  • For endometrial cancer, MRI shows the depth of myometrial invasion and whether the cervical stroma is involved.
  • PET changes the radiation map: a positive pelvic node gets a boost, a para-aortic node means an extended field, and distant disease can change the treatment intent.
  • For cervical brachytherapy, an MRI or CT with the applicator in place is used to contour the residual tumor and the bladder, rectum, and sigmoid, then cover the tumor while respecting those organs.

Workup & Staging.title: Gynecologic Cancer Workup & FIGO Staging
Workup & Staging.html:
How to Stage Any GYN Cancer

Staging is how you classify the extent and risk of a cancer so the team can choose surgery, radiation, or systemic therapy. Work through it in the same order every time:

1
Identify the organ
→
2
Local extent: what does the tumor touch?
→
3
Nodes, then distant disease
→
4
Apply that site's FIGO system
CancerWhat you really need to determine
CervixSize, parametria, vagina, side wall or hydronephrosis, nodes
EndometriumHistology and grade, myometrial invasion, LVSI, cervical stroma, nodes, molecular group
VulvaTumor size and depth of invasion, adjacent structures (urethra, vagina, anus), groin nodes
VaginaLocation and extent, adjacent structures, pelvic vs groin nodes

As a rough orientation, the FIGO stages tend to move outward: stage I in the organ, stage II into an adjacent structure, stage III toward the side wall or nodes, stage IV into the bladder or rectal mucosa or distant sites. Treat that as a pattern, not the rule: what counts as "adjacent" or "stage III" is defined differently for each site, so always apply the site's own system.

Two findings work the same way at all four sites on this page:

  • A positive regional node makes it at least stage III (cervix IIIC, endometrium IIIC, vulva IIIA–C, vagina III), no matter how small the primary.
  • Bullous edema of the bladder is not stage IV. You need tumor in the mucosa, proven on biopsy.

How Each Site Is Staged, at a Glance

Site Staging basis The cutoffs and findings that change the stage
Cervix Clinical + imaging + pathology (FIGO 2018) Depth (3, 5 mm), size (2, 4 cm), parametria, lower vagina, hydronephrosis, nodes (pelvic vs para-aortic)
Endometrium Surgical (FIGO 2023, which adds histology, LVSI, and molecular group to the 2009 anatomic stages) Myometrial depth (50%), cervical stroma, serosa/adnexa, nodes; plus grade, histology, LVSI, molecular class
Vulva Surgical (FIGO 2021) 2 cm size, 1 mm depth, lower vs upper urethra/vagina/anus, node size (5 mm), extracapsular spread
Vagina Clinical (FIGO) Vaginal wall → paravaginal tissue → pelvic side wall → bladder/rectum; any pelvic or inguinal node = III

Why the basis differs: cervix and vagina are staged before surgery because many patients go straight to chemoradiation, so the stage has to be assignable by exam and imaging. Endometrium and vulva are staged after surgery because the defining facts (myometrial depth, node status, depth of invasion) come from the specimen.

Cervical Cancer: FIGO 2018

Staging basis: clinical exam + imaging + pathology. Imaging and pathology may supplement the clinical findings, and pathology supersedes imaging and exam (Bhatla et al., FIGO 2018).

Workup (What Feeds the Stage)

  1. History and pelvic/rectovaginal exam (± exam under anesthesia): tumor size, vaginal extension, parametrial thickening.
  2. Cervical biopsy, or cone biopsy for microscopic disease.
  3. Pelvic MRI for local extent; FDG-PET/CT for nodes and distant disease (preferred for IB1–IB3) (NCCN Cervical Cancer, v2.2026).
  4. Labs: CBC, renal and liver function (cisplatin, hydronephrosis), HIV testing.
  5. Cystoscopy or proctoscopy only if bladder or rectal invasion is suspected.
  6. Fertility and smoking-cessation counseling.

Build the Stage Up

  • Stage I: in the cervix. Sized first by depth (microscopic disease), then by diameter.
    • IA (microscopic only): IA1 ≤3 mm deep · IA2 >3 to ≤5 mm deep.
    • IB (>5 mm deep or visible): IB1 ≤2 cm · IB2 >2 to ≤4 cm · IB3 >4 cm.
  • Stage II: just beyond the uterus. IIA upper two-thirds of the vagina, no parametria (IIA1 ≤4 cm · IIA2 >4 cm) · IIB parametria, not to the side wall.
  • Stage III: walls or nodes. IIIA lower third of the vagina · IIIB pelvic side wall and/or hydronephrosis · IIIC nodes (IIIC1 pelvic · IIIC2 para-aortic), with an r (imaging) or p (pathology) suffix.
  • Stage IV: mucosa or distant. IVA bladder or rectal mucosa (biopsy-proven) · IVB distant.

The Memory Hooks

  • Size cutoffs are 2 and 4 cm. Depth cutoffs are 3 and 5 mm.
  • Parametria = IIB. Lower vagina = IIIA. Side wall or hydronephrosis = IIIB. Any node = IIIC.
  • IIIC is heterogeneous by design: a 1.5 cm tumor with one positive pelvic node is IIIC1, the same stage label as a bulky tumor with nodes. This is a known weakness of the 2018 system (Wright et al., Obstetrics & Gynecology, 2019).

Classic Traps

  • A node makes it IIIC no matter how small the primary is.
  • Bullous edema is not IVA; you need a mucosal biopsy.
  • IB2 is a swing stage: surgery and definitive radiation are both reasonable. Choose the strategy most likely to cure with the least unnecessary multimodality toxicity.
Quick check: 3.8 cm tumor, parametria clear on MRI, PET shows a positive external iliac node. Stage?▾

Size alone would suggest IB2, but the positive pelvic node makes it IIIC1r.

Endometrial Cancer: FIGO 2023 and the Anatomic Backbone

Staging basis: surgical/pathologic. Endometrial staging has evolved beyond the traditional 2009 anatomic system: modern FIGO staging (2023) incorporates histology, LVSI, and molecular features in selected stages. The 2009 stages (IA, IB, II, and so on) are still the backbone, and you will hear them on rounds, in older trials, and in guidelines that have not fully adopted 2023, so learn the anatomy first and then the modifiers.

Workup (What Feeds the Stage)

  1. Endometrial biopsy or D&C for histology and grade.
  2. Molecular testing on every tumor: MMR/MSI, p53, and POLE; add ER/PR, and HER2 for serous or p53-abnormal tumors (NCCN Uterine Neoplasms, v3.2026).
  3. Imaging: chest imaging; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for high-grade or advanced disease; pelvic MRI for local extent or inoperable patients.
  4. CA-125 for serous or suspected extrauterine disease; genetic counseling for MMR-deficient tumors (Lynch).
  5. Surgical staging: total hysterectomy + bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy + sentinel node mapping (± omentectomy for serous).

The Anatomic Backbone (FIGO 2009)

  • Stage I: in the uterine body. IA <50% myometrial invasion · IB ≥50%.
  • Stage II: cervical stroma (glands alone don't count).
  • Stage III: regional. IIIA serosa or adnexa · IIIB vagina or parametria · IIIC1 pelvic nodes · IIIC2 para-aortic nodes.
  • Stage IV: mucosa or distant. IVA bladder or bowel mucosa · IVB distant (including intra-abdominal and inguinal nodes).

What Actually Drives Treatment (Why the 2023 Update Exists)

Anatomic stage alone under-predicts how endometrial cancer behaves. These modifiers drive the recurrence-risk assessment, and with it the adjuvant therapy:

Grade & Histology

Grade 1–2 endometrioid = low grade; grade 3, serous, clear cell, and carcinosarcoma = high risk.

LVSI

Substantial LVSI strongly predicts nodal and pelvic recurrence.

Age

Older age raises risk (the GOG-99 and PORTEC-1 cutoffs of 50, 60, and 70).

Molecular Class

POLEmut (excellent prognosis) · MMRd (intermediate; immunotherapy-responsive) · NSMP (intermediate) · p53abn (worst).

What FIGO 2023 Changed (the Logic, Not the List)

FIGO 2023 folds tumor biology into the stage, so biology can override pure anatomy (Berek et al., FIGO 2023):

  • Histology and LVSI now enter stage II: aggressive histology with any myometrial invasion = IIC; substantial LVSI = IIB; aggressive histology with no invasion = IC.
  • Molecular override, for stage I–II only:
    • POLE-mutated → downstaged to IAmPOLEmut (favorable, even if high grade or deeply invasive).
    • p53-abnormal with myometrial invasion → upstaged to IICmp53abn (aggressive even when anatomically confined).
  • Stage III–IV are not reclassified by molecular class (How et al., Nat Rev Clin Oncol, 2024).
Quick check (anatomic stage): grade 2 endometrioid, 70% myometrial invasion, tumor in the cervical glands but not the stroma, nodes negative. Stage?▾

IB. Deep invasion (≥50%) makes it IB, and cervical glandular involvement does not upstage it (stage II needs the stroma).

Vulvar Cancer: FIGO 2021

Staging basis: surgical. Node status is the single most important determinant of survival (NCCN Vulvar Cancer, v2.2026).

Workup (What Feeds the Stage)

  1. Biopsy (punch or wedge, not excision) so the depth of invasion can be measured on intact tissue.
  2. Exam of the groins, vagina, cervix, and anus: HPV-related disease is often multifocal.
  3. Imaging (pelvic MRI, CT, or PET/CT) for tumors >4 cm, suspicious groin nodes, or advanced disease; groin ultrasound ± FNA.
  4. Exam under anesthesia with cystoscopy/proctoscopy for advanced disease; HIV testing.

Build the Stage Up

  • Stage I: on the vulva/perineum. IA ≤2 cm and ≤1 mm invasion, so groin evaluation can be omitted (<1% node risk). IB >2 cm or >1 mm invasion.
  • Stage II: lower adjacent structures. Any size into the lower third of the urethra, vagina, or anus, with negative nodes.
  • Stage III: upper structures or nodes. IIIA upper two-thirds of the urethra/vagina, bladder or rectal mucosa, or regional nodes ≤5 mm · IIIB nodes >5 mm · IIIC nodes with extracapsular spread.
  • Stage IV: fixed or distant. IVA fixed to pelvic bone, or fixed/ulcerated groin nodes · IVB distant (including pelvic nodes).

The Memory Hooks

  • Two numbers for the primary: 2 cm (size) and 1 mm (depth). Both small and shallow = IA.
  • Lower third of the urethra/vagina/anus = II; upper two-thirds = IIIA.
  • The node story is a size ladder: ≤5 mm = IIIA · >5 mm = IIIB · extracapsular = IIIC · fixed/ulcerated = IVA.

Classic Trap

Depth of invasion decides whether groin surgery is needed, and the 2021 depth-measurement method can downstage some tumors to IA, which may miss nodal disease. Correlate carefully with the clinical node findings (van der Kolk et al., Eur J Cancer, 2026).

Vaginal Cancer: FIGO

Staging basis: clinical. First, prove it is actually a vaginal primary. By FIGO definition, a tumor involving the cervix is a cervical cancer, and one involving the vulva is a vulvar cancer. Most lesions in the vagina are secondary (metastatic), not true vaginal primaries (NCCN Vaginal Cancer, v2.2026).

Workup (What Feeds the Stage)

  1. History and physical with sexual history, immunosuppression, prior hysterectomy, and smoking.
  2. Pelvic exam (bimanual + rectovaginal), cervical/Pap evaluation, colposcopy, and vulvar exam, to exclude a cervical or vulvar primary.
  3. Exam under anesthesia with biopsies (± cystoscopy/proctoscopy) as indicated; imaging (MRI preferred for local extent).
  4. CBC, CMP; HPV and HIV testing in select patients.

Build the Stage Up

  • Stage I: in the vaginal wall (T1a ≤2 cm · T1b >2 cm).
  • Stage II: paravaginal tissue, not to the pelvic side wall.
  • Stage III: pelvic side wall and/or hydronephrosis, or any pelvic or inguinal node (N1).
  • Stage IVA: bladder or rectal mucosa, or beyond the true pelvis (bullous edema is not enough) · IVB: distant.

The Memory Hook

Walk the tumor outward: wall (I) → paravaginal tissue (II) → side wall, hydronephrosis, or a node (III) → bladder/rectum or distant (IV). It is essentially cervical-cancer logic applied to the vaginal tube.

Four Reflexes to Carry onto Rounds

1

Organ first, then local extent, nodes, and distant disease; only then apply that site's FIGO system and worry about the substage letter.

2

See a positive regional node, think at least stage III for cervix, endometrium, vulva, and vagina.

3

Bullous edema is never enough for stage IV: demand a mucosal biopsy.

4

For the vagina, confirm it isn't really cervix or vulva before you stage it at all.

Full FIGO tables and the NCCN workup algorithms for each site are reproduced at the bottom of this page.

High-Yield Summary
  • Stage any GYN cancer by identifying the organ, then the local extent, nodes, and distant disease, and only then applying that site's FIGO system.
  • A positive regional node makes a cervical, endometrial, vulvar, or vaginal cancer at least stage III, no matter how small the primary tumor is.
  • Cervix and vagina are staged clinically with exam and imaging, while endometrium and vulva are staged surgically from the specimen.
  • In the cervix, depth cutoffs are 3 and 5 mm and size cutoffs are 2 and 4 cm; parametria is IIB, lower vagina IIIA, side wall or hydronephrosis IIIB, and nodes IIIC.
  • Modern FIGO endometrial staging adds histology, LVSI, and molecular group to the older anatomic stages, so the 2009 IA and IB system is the backbone, not the complete picture.

Treatment Paradigms.title: Gynecologic Cancer Treatment Paradigms
Treatment Paradigms.html:
A woman with a GYN cancer walks into your clinic. By now you know what she has (Epidemiology), where it can spread (Anatomy), where it is (Imaging), and its stage and risk (Workup & Staging). Treatment asks the last question: what does radiation actually do for this patient? Three questions get you there:

1
What is the definitive local treatment?

Small, confined, operable disease → usually surgery (or definitive RT for the cervix). Locally advanced disease → definitive chemoradiation.

2
After surgery, what did pathology show?

Risk features (margins, nodes, depth, LVSI, histology, molecular group) decide observation, brachytherapy, pelvic RT, or chemoRT.

3
What must the radiation cover?

The primary or vaginal cuff, then the nodes at risk: pelvis, para-aortics if they're involved or at high risk, groins for the vulva and lower vagina.

Whenever possible, choose the definitive local treatment that avoids unnecessary multimodality toxicity. Surgery followed by adjuvant RT or chemoradiation is appropriate when the pathology shows features that warrant it.

The Big Picture by Site

SiteEarly / confinedLocally advanced or node-positiveWhere radiation fits
CervixRadical hysterectomy or definitive RTChemoRT + brachytherapyThe main curative treatment for most patients
EndometriumHysterectomy + BSO + sentinel nodesSurgery → systemic therapy ± RTMostly adjuvant: vaginal brachy or pelvic EBRT
VulvaRadical local excision + groin stagingChemoRT (adjuvant or definitive)Adjuvant for nodes or margins; definitive when surgery would be too morbid
VaginaRT (brachy ± EBRT)EBRT ± chemo + brachyThe main treatment

Why Brachytherapy Matters So Much in GYN

The applicator sits inside the body, right against the tumor: in the cervical canal and vaginal fornices, or in the vagina after hysterectomy. That puts a very high dose directly into and around the cervix and residual tumor, with rapid dose falloff before the bladder, rectum, and sigmoid. External beam can't match that.

Intact cervix
Tandem + ring or ovoids ± needles
  • Given near the end of or after EBRT, once the tumor has shrunk
  • Delivers the curative dose to the cervix
  • Essential: an IMRT or SBRT boost is not an equivalent substitute
  • Interstitial needles for bulky or parametrial residual disease
After hysterectomy
Vaginal cylinder (cuff)
  • Treats the vaginal cuff, the most common place endometrial cancer recurs
  • Used alone, or as a boost after pelvic EBRT
  • Few side effects: mainly vaginal dryness and narrowing
Planning details: representative regimens you'll hear on rounds▾
SettingRepresentative examples
Pelvic EBRT (IMRT)45–50.4 Gy in 25–28 fractions; extended field for para-aortic disease
Concurrent chemoWeekly cisplatin 40 mg/m²
Gross nodal boostAbout 55–60 Gy, often as a simultaneous integrated boost
Intact cervix HDR brachye.g., 7 Gy × 4 or 6 Gy × 5, aiming for HR-CTV D90 ≥85 Gy EQD2
Vaginal cuff brachy alonee.g., 7 Gy × 3 at 0.5 cm depth (PORTEC-2 style)
Vaginal cuff brachy after EBRTe.g., 5–6 Gy × 2–3

Regimens vary by institution and protocol; learn the pattern, not the menu.

Track 1: Cervix

The cervix is the centerpiece of GYN radiation oncology: it is the disease where radiation is most often the curative treatment. The path runs early → postoperative → locally advanced → recurrent or metastatic.

Early-Stage, Operable (roughly IA–IB2, IIA1)

Option 1
Surgery

Radical hysterectomy + pelvic node evaluation (sentinel nodes), done open. Selected low-risk tumors can have a simple hysterectomy, and young patients with small tumors may have a fertility-sparing trachelectomy.

Option 2
Definitive RT

EBRT + brachytherapy ± cisplatin. Survival is similar to surgery (Landoni). Often chosen for poor surgical candidates, or when the tumor looks likely to need adjuvant RT anyway.

The central decision is surgery or definitive RT. Tiny microinvasive tumors (IA1 without LVSI) need only a cone or simple hysterectomy.

After Surgery: What Did the Pathology Show?

  • No risk features → observation.
  • Intermediate risk (a combination of LVSI, deep stromal invasion, and tumor size: the Sedlis criteria) → postoperative pelvic RT.
  • High risk (positive nodes, positive margins, or parametrial invasion: the Peters criteria) → postoperative concurrent chemoradiation.
Postoperative cervix: Sedlis & Peters, know this for rounds▾
Intermediate risk
Sedlis criteria → pelvic RT
LVSIStromal invasionSize
+Deep thirdAny
+Middle third≥2 cm
+Superficial third≥5 cm
−Middle or deep third≥4 cm

GOG 92: pelvic RT cut recurrence roughly in half.

High risk
Peters criteria → chemoRT
  • Positive nodes
  • Positive margins
  • Parametrial invasion

GOG 109: adding chemo to pelvic RT improved overall survival.

Use the checker below to practice.

Try it: 2.5 cm tumor, LVSI present, superficial third invasion, nodes and margins negative. Adjuvant?▾

Observation. LVSI with superficial invasion needs a tumor ≥5 cm to meet Sedlis. No Peters features.

Locally Advanced (roughly IB3, IIA2, IIB–IVA): The Signature Pathway

1
Pelvic EBRT + weekly cisplatin
→
2
Brachytherapy to the cervix and residual tumor
→
3
Finish the whole course promptly (about 8 weeks)
→
4
Response PET a few months later
  • Concurrent chemotherapy improves survival over RT alone.
  • Brachytherapy is essential; external beam alone is not an equivalent substitute for the intracavitary or interstitial component.
  • Don't let the course drag on. Prolonged overall treatment time lowers local control, so breaks are avoided and brachytherapy is scheduled tightly.
  • No routine hysterectomy after chemoRT.

Node-Positive: PET Draws the Field

  • Pelvic nodes: the same chemoRT + brachytherapy, with a boost to the involved nodes. Many add the para-aortics for common iliac or multiple pelvic nodes.
  • Para-aortic nodes: extended-field chemoRT, with nodal boosts. The kidneys, duodenum, and bowel now enter the plan.
  • Nodes found at surgery: the radical hysterectomy is often abandoned in favor of definitive chemoRT rather than finishing a morbid operation that will need chemoRT anyway.

What the Radiation Treats (Definitive Cervix)

You don't need to contour on a sub-I, but you should know what the team is drawing and why.

PTVA margin for daily setup uncertainty
ITVCovers how the uterus and cervix move with bladder and rectal filling
CTVCervix, uterus, parametria, and upper vagina, plus the elective pelvic nodes (± para-aortics)
GTVThe primary tumor plus involved nodes (boosted)
While protecting
  • Bladder
  • Rectum
  • Sigmoid
  • Small bowel
  • Bone marrow
  • Femoral heads
  • Kidneys (extended field)

After a hysterectomy the target is the vaginal cuff, upper vagina, parametria, and pelvic nodes instead of the intact uterus. The brachytherapy target (HR-CTV) is covered in Imaging.

Recurrent or Metastatic

  • Systemic therapy (chemotherapy with immunotherapy ± bevacizumab) is the backbone for metastatic disease.
  • Palliative RT stops vaginal bleeding and treats pain, often in a short course.
  • Limited distant disease (e.g., a single supraclavicular node) is sometimes treated with curative intent.
  • Central pelvic recurrence after RT: consider pelvic exenteration. Pelvic recurrence after surgery alone: chemoRT.

Track 2: Endometrium

The radiation oncology question for endometrial cancer is almost always: why does this patient need radiation after surgery? Surgery (hysterectomy, BSO, sentinel nodes) establishes the pathology and the risk. Then read the report:

1
The tumor

Histology (endometrioid vs serous, clear cell, carcinosarcoma) and grade.

2
How far it went

Depth of myometrial invasion, cervical stroma, and nodes.

3
How it spreads

LVSI, especially when substantial.

4
Biology and patient

Molecular group, then age and other clinical factors.

Endometrial adjuvant therapy rises with recurrence risk

Go top to bottom.

1
If the recurrence risk is…
Low
Observation.
e.g., low-grade endometrioid, superficial invasion, no substantial LVSI; also many POLE-mutated tumors.
2
If the recurrence risk is…
Intermediate, mostly at the vaginal cuff
Often vaginal brachytherapy (or observation).
e.g., deeper invasion or higher grade, especially in older patients.
3
If the risk extends to…
The pelvic nodes and side wall
Pelvic EBRT (± vaginal brachy).
e.g., substantial LVSI, cervical stromal invasion, high grade with deep invasion.
4
If the patient has…
High-risk biology or stage III or higher
Systemic therapy ± pelvic RT, based on the risk and where the disease was.
e.g., serous or p53-abnormal tumors, positive nodes.
  • Molecular group moves patients up or down the ladder: POLE-mutated tumors are candidates for de-escalation, and p53-abnormal tumors for escalation.
  • Most early-stage recurrences are at the vaginal cuff, which is why vaginal brachytherapy is so common: PORTEC-2 showed it controlled the vagina as well as pelvic EBRT with far less bowel toxicity.
  • Node-positive disease is systemic-therapy led; pelvic RT is often added for pelvic and vaginal control (PORTEC-3, GOG 258). Immunotherapy added to chemo helps advanced disease, especially MMR-deficient tumors.
  • Medically inoperable patients (e.g., severe obesity or heart disease): definitive brachytherapy ± EBRT, with MRI to define the extent.

Track 3: Vulva

Vulva drains to the groins. Every vulvar plan is really two questions: the vulva, and the groins.
  • Small, unifocal, clinically node-negative → radical local excision + sentinel node evaluation when appropriate (lateral tumors: same-side groin; midline: both groins). Only tiny, very superficial tumors (stage IA) skip the groins.
  • Positive nodes or adverse pathology (multiple nodes, extracapsular extension, close or positive margins that can't be re-excised) → groin ± pelvic RT, often with cisplatin, ± RT to the vulva.
  • Locally advanced disease where surgery would be mutilating (it would remove the urethra, anus, or clitoris, or need an exenteration) → definitive chemoradiation, which can preserve anatomy and function. Residual disease is biopsied and resected if feasible.
Planning details: vulvar adjuvant thresholds and doses▾
  • Adjuvant groin + pelvic RT: ≥2 positive nodes, extracapsular extension, or a sentinel node metastasis >2 mm. A sentinel micrometastasis (≤2 mm) can be treated with groin RT alone (GROINSS-V II).
  • Close margins: historically <8 mm; re-excision first if possible.
  • Adjuvant doses about 45–50.4 Gy, higher (about 54–64 Gy) for extracapsular extension or positive margins.
  • Definitive chemoRT: about 57.6–64 Gy to the vulva with weekly cisplatin; gross nodes higher.
GOG 37

For node-positive vulvar cancer, groin and pelvic RT beat pelvic node dissection.

GOG 205

Definitive chemoRT with weekly cisplatin produced high complete response rates in locally advanced disease, sparing many patients an exenteration.

Track 4: Vagina

  • Rare. First exclude a cervical or vulvar primary, or a metastasis.
  • Location matters: the upper vagina drains to the pelvic nodes; the lower vagina drains to the groins, which are added to the field.
  • RT is central. Very superficial stage I lesions can be treated with brachytherapy alone; most invasive lesions get EBRT (± cisplatin) + brachytherapy, borrowing the cervix approach.
  • Thick or irregular disease needs interstitial brachytherapy (needles), because a cylinder can't reach deep enough.
Other GYN Cancers: Quick Reference

Ovarian, fallopian tube, and primary peritoneal cancer are treated with surgery and chemotherapy; radiation is mostly palliative (bleeding, pain, or a symptomatic mass). Uterine sarcomas and other rare tumors are surgery-led, with radiation used selectively.

Organs at Risk: Know What You're Protecting

Every organ at risk in the plan maps to a side effect you'll counsel patients about. Knowing that link is what makes the plan make sense.

RectumProctitis and bleeding

Bone marrowLow blood counts, which can force cisplatin to be held

Femoral headsFracture, especially with groin fields

Toxicity: What to Counsel

During treatment
  • Fatigue
  • Diarrhea and cramping
  • Urinary frequency and burning
  • Low blood counts, especially with cisplatin
  • Skin reaction, which is severe with vulvar and groin RT
Months to years later
  • Vaginal stenosis and dryness
  • Sexual dysfunction
  • Bowel injury (bleeding, stricture) and bladder injury
  • Fistula (rare)
  • Lymphedema, especially after node dissection plus RT
  • Pelvic insufficiency fractures
  • Ovarian failure (premature menopause); consider ovarian transposition in young patients having surgery
Clinical Pearl

Vaginal dilator counseling and sexual health are part of survivorship care, not an afterthought. Ask about them at every follow-up visit.

The Evidence: Why These Trials Matter

1999 Cisplatin Trials
Question
Does concurrent chemotherapy improve RT for locally advanced cervical cancer?
Result
Yes: a substantially lower risk of death (GOG 85, 120, 123, RTOG 9001, SWOG 8797).
Why it matters
Concurrent cisplatin with RT is standard.
LACC
Question
Is minimally invasive radical hysterectomy as good as open surgery?
Result
No: worse disease-free and overall survival with the laparoscopic or robotic approach.
Why it matters
Radical hysterectomy for cervical cancer is done open.
SHAPE
Question
Do low-risk early cervical cancers need a radical hysterectomy?
Result
A simple hysterectomy was noninferior for pelvic recurrence in selected small, low-risk tumors.
Why it matters
Less surgery for selected low-risk disease.
EMBRACE
Question
What does MRI-guided brachytherapy achieve?
Result
High local control, with target dose linked to control and OAR dose linked to toxicity.
Why it matters
Modern image-guided brachytherapy and its dose goals.
PORTEC-2
Question
For intermediate-risk endometrial cancer, is vaginal brachy enough?
Result
Vaginal brachy controlled the vagina as well as pelvic EBRT, with far less GI toxicity (building on PORTEC-1 and GOG 99, where pelvic RT cut mostly vaginal recurrences without a survival gain).
Why it matters
Why selected patients get the cylinder instead of the pelvis.
PORTEC-3 & GOG 258
Question
Chemo, RT, or both for high-risk or stage III endometrial cancer?
Result
ChemoRT beat RT alone, mostly in stage III and serous/p53-abnormal tumors (PORTEC-3); adding RT to chemo lowered vaginal and pelvic recurrences (GOG 258).
Why it matters
High-risk disease is multimodality.
Recent and advanced updates▾
INTERLACE

A short course of induction carboplatin and paclitaxel before chemoRT improved survival in locally advanced cervical cancer; some centers use it.

KEYNOTE-A18

Pembrolizumab during and after chemoRT improved progression-free and overall survival in high-risk locally advanced cervical cancer.

KEYNOTE-826

Pembrolizumab added to chemotherapy for persistent, recurrent, or metastatic cervical cancer (PD-L1 positive).

RUBY & NRG-GY018

Immunotherapy (dostarlimab, pembrolizumab) added to chemo for advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer, with the largest benefit in MMR-deficient tumors.

GYN guidelines are changing quickly, so check the current versions for real patients.

High-Yield Summary
  • Choose the definitive local treatment that avoids unnecessary multimodality toxicity, and add adjuvant RT or chemoradiation after surgery only when the pathology warrants it.
  • Locally advanced cervical cancer gets pelvic EBRT with concurrent cisplatin plus brachytherapy, and brachytherapy is essential because it puts a high dose into the cervix with rapid falloff.
  • After radical hysterectomy, intermediate-risk pathology (Sedlis) leads to pelvic RT, and positive nodes, margins, or parametria (Peters) lead to chemoradiation.
  • Endometrial cancer radiation is decided after surgery by recurrence risk: observation, vaginal brachytherapy, pelvic EBRT, or systemic therapy with or without RT, adjusted by molecular group.
  • Vulvar cancer drains to the groins, gets excision with groin staging, adjuvant groin and pelvic RT for adverse nodes, and definitive chemoradiation when surgery would be mutilating.
